title: When something goes wrong
job: Problems, asking for help, complaining calmly
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: mot OPENS HERE, and L1 named it as deferred with one mention. The law in one line: an is DO NOT or WILL NOT, mot is CANNOT. mot gayo means something is stopping me; an gayo means I am choosing not to. English's single "can't" and "won't" hide the difference, and a problem report is the only place in the ladder where both are needed in the same breath.

Pain and malfunction both use the DOUBLE-SUBJECT sentence M2 taught: meori-ga apayo (my head hurts — as-for-me, the head hurts) and i-geo-ga an dwaeyo (this does not work). apayo is a descriptive verb like everything in M2 and M3, so nothing new is opened here; a structure is APPLIED for the third time. A learner who sees the third use learns the structure; a learner given three idioms learns three idioms.

-eoya dwaeyo is the OBLIGATION ending: gayaa dwaeyo, gidaryeoya dwaeyo. It is built on the same -a/-eo stem the course has been conjugating since L1-M4, so the shape is familiar and only the frame is new. With M1's dowajuseyo and M1's ability question, that is the whole kit a problem needs and no new tense is opened for any of it.

COMPLAINING CALMLY, and Korean's answer is the HONORIFIC rather than the hedge. The softening comes from M1's jom, from joesonghajiman ("I'm sorry, but"), and from keeping the honorific on the person you are complaining TO. Raising your voice with a stranger is a heavier breach in Korean than in English, and the repair is the ending, not the volume.

dwaeyo is M7's row doing its widest job: it becomes, it works, it will do. an dwaeyo is the everyday "it's not working" and also "that won't do" — one verb covering a broken machine and a refused request, and the sentence decides which.

words.note: M7's dwaeyo with L1-M3's an. It covers a broken machine and a refused request alike, and the sentence around it says which — i-geo-ga an dwaeyo, jeonhwa-ga an dwaeyo.

sentences.trap: an and not mot, because a machine is not being prevented from anything — it simply does not work. mot belongs to a person who is stopped by something, and that is the whole of the difference.
sentences.sound: i-GEO-ga an DWAE-yo. an is short and runs straight into the verb.

variations.changed: on its own — a refusal rather than a fault

mistake.why: A machine is not prevented, it just fails: I-geo-ga an dwaeyo.

sentences.usage: At a counter, a machine, a rented room.

words.note: The inability negative, and it goes in front of the verb exactly as L1-M3's an does. mot gayo means something is stopping you; an gayo means you have decided not to.

sentences.trap: English's 'I can't come' is ambiguous and Korean's is not. mot gayo says something outside you is in the way; an gayo says you are not going, and a listener hears the difference immediately.
sentences.sound: O-neul mot GA-yo. The t of mot is unreleased and hardens the g after it.

variations.changed: a choice rather than an obstacle

mistake.why: The inability negative is mot: Oneul mot gayo.

sentences.usage: Cancelling, and the word choice says whether it was your decision.
sentences.mnemonic: mot is stopped. an is chose not to.

words.note: A descriptive verb like every other, so M2's double subject builds this sentence with nothing new in it. Its modifier is apeun.

sentences.trap: This is M2's structure for the third time: the topic is you and the SUBJECT is the part that hurts. Nothing here says 'my' and nothing needs to — the sentence is about you already.
sentences.sound: MEO-ri-ga a-PA-yo. Both words are three light syllables.

mistake.why: The part that hurts is the subject: Meori-ga apayo.

sentences.usage: At a chemist, or explaining why you are going home.
sentences.mnemonic: The part hurts. You are only the topic.

words.note: ireo-, to lose, plus -beorida, which says the thing is gone for good. L1-M5's past sits on the end of it and nothing else is new.

sentences.trap: -beorida adds regret and finality, which English carries with 'gone' rather than with a verb ending. Korean puts it inside the verb, and a learner who leaves it out sounds oddly unbothered.
sentences.sound: GA-bang-eul i-reo-beo-RYEO-sseo-yo. Six syllables, and the ryeo carries the stress.

variations.cue: I've lost my bag. Please help me.

mistake.why: What you lost is an object: Gabang-eul ireobeoryeosseoyo.

sentences.usage: At a lost-property desk, or a station office.
sentences.mnemonic: -beorida means it is gone, and you mind.

sentences.cue: I have to go to the hospital.

words.note: Any medical place, from a big hospital to a one-room clinic — Korean draws no line where English draws one.
The obligation frame: the -a/-eo stem the course has conjugated since L1-M4, plus -ya, plus dwaeyo. Only the frame is new.

sentences.trap: -e and not -eseo, because the hospital is where you are GOING. M4's law again, and it holds in every module that follows it.
sentences.sound: BYEONG-wo-ne GA-ya DWAE-yo. byeong is one syllable.

variations.changed: medicine, which in Korean is eaten

variations.cue: Can you get to a hospital?

mistake.why: A destination takes -e: Byeongwon-e gaya dwaeyo.

sentences.usage: Explaining why you have to leave.
sentences.mnemonic: -eoya dwaeyo: you must. Nothing new but the frame.

words.note: Korean EATS medicine — yak-eul meokda — where English takes it. The verb is L1-M3's meokda and nothing about it changes.

sentences.trap: Medicine is eaten in Korean, not taken. It is one of the clearest cases where the verb a language picks is simply a fact about that language, and translating 'take' gives a sentence nobody says.
sentences.sound: YA-geul meo-GEO-ya DWAE-yo. The k of yak runs into the particle.

mistake.why: Medicine is eaten in Korean: Yak-eul meogeoya dwaeyo.

sentences.usage: At a pharmacy, which in Korea is on every second corner.

sentences.cue: I'm sorry, but this is broken.

words.note: M1's joesonghamnida with L1-M10's -jiman, 'but'. It opens a complaint and is what makes the rest of it acceptable.
The noun for something being broken, and gojang-ieyo is the sign you will see on a machine. an dwaeyo is the spoken version.

sentences.trap: THE SOFTENING IS THE OPENING, not a weakening of the complaint. Korean states the fault plainly after joesonghajiman, and an English speaker who hedges the fault itself instead sounds evasive rather than polite.

variations.cue: I'm sorry, but could you help me?
variations.changed: a request rather than a complaint
without the opening — plain, and not rude

variations.cue: I'm sorry, but I can't come now.

mistake.why: Korean softens at the front and states the fault plainly: Joesonghajiman, i-geo-ga gojang-ieyo.

sentences.usage: Opening a complaint at a desk, calmly.
sentences.mnemonic: Soften the opening. State the fault flat.

words.note: M1's dowajuseyo rebuilt on M6's invitation ending, which turns an instruction into a question about the listener's wish — and that is what makes it softer.

sentences.trap: Asking whether somebody WANTS to help is softer than asking them to help, and Korean builds that softness into the ending rather than into extra words. English does the same with 'would you' and then adds four more words anyway.
sentences.sound: jom do-wa-joo-sil-LAE-yo. Six syllables, level throughout.

variations.changed: M1's plain request, which is not rude

mistake.why: Asking a stranger keeps the honorific: Jom dowajusillae-yo?

sentences.usage: To a stranger, when something has gone wrong.
sentences.mnemonic: Ask what they WANT, not what they will do.

words.note: Always in the PAST, because the injury has already happened — Korean reports the event and English reports the state. L1-M5's -eoss- again.

sentences.trap: English says 'I am hurt' and Korean says 'I got hurt'. The past is not optional here: the present would say you are in the act of injuring yourself.
sentences.sound: da-CHYEO-sseo-yo. The chyeo is one syllable.

variations.changed: somebody else, with the subject particle

variations.cue: I'm hurt. I have to go to hospital.

sentences.usage: Said quickly, and it will get attention.
sentences.mnemonic: Korean reports the event. English reports the state.

words.note: M1's gidaryeojuseyo without the juseyo half — the plain verb, doing its own work. gidaryeoya dwaeyo is the obligation shape.

sentences.trap: mot puts the reason outside you and an puts it inside. Here mot says a train or a meeting is forcing your hand, which is exactly what makes it a courteous thing to say.
sentences.sound: JI-geum mot gi-da-RYEO-yo. The t of mot hardens the g.

variations.changed: a choice, which lands very differently

mistake.why: mot goes with a plain verb, not a request: Jigeum mot gidaryeoyo.

sentences.usage: Leaving a queue, or getting off a call.
sentences.mnemonic: mot blames the world. an blames you.

comprehensionPool.cue: I have to go to the hospital.
I'm sorry, but this is broken.
